say: The danger of a QR code is that you cannot read a URL you cannot see — you point your phone and trust it. This tool decodes the code from a photo, or lets you paste the link directly, then inspects the destination's structure for phishing tells. It never visits the link — the analysis is pure text, safe by construction.
Here is a link of exactly the kind a fake parking-fine or delivery QR carries. Let me paste it in rather than a photo.
Check the URL. The structural heuristics run locally, and the destination is also looked up against Google Safe Browsing's known-threat database.

High risk — and three concrete reasons, not a vague score. The at-sign trick, where everything before the @ is ignored by the browser so the real host is the lookalike after it. A one-character typosquat of paypal-dot-com. And plain HTTP. Each is a verifiable fact about the link itself.

The honest limit, stated on the page: these are red flags in the link's structure, not a verdict on the page behind it. A link with no flags can still be malicious — a freshly registered but plausible domain this can't see. The real advice is behavioural: don't scan unfamiliar QR codes in public, and never enter credentials after following one.
